title: The Ba'iyya of Abu Tammam
intro: Abu Tammam wrote this ode for the caliph al-Mu'tasim when he took Amorium, a Byzantine stronghold in Anatolia, in 223 AH (838 CE). Al-Tibrizi, opening his commentary on it, says that the astrologers had ruled that the caliph would not take the city, and that the Byzantines wrote to him that their books said it could fall only when the figs and grapes were ripe; he refused to leave until it fell. The poem opens, with no prelude, by mocking the astrologers, then pictures the city as a virgin untouched since Alexander and the fire that turned its night to day, praises the caliph, recalls the woman of Zibatra whose cry for help he answered and the Byzantine emperor's flight, and ends by setting his victory beside the Prophet's at Badr. It is dense with antithesis and wordplay, which al-Suli and al-Tibrizi point out line by line, and its opening half-line is quoted to this day. It is known as the Ba'iyya of Abu Tammam, “the poem in ba'”, after its rhyme.

translation: The sword is truer in its tidings than the books;
its edge is the line between earnest and play.
1.sharh: The sword told the truth about Amorium, where the books had said it would not fall. Its edge (hadd) is also the dividing line (hadd) between earnest and jest: once it is drawn, the talking stops.

translation: White blades, not black pages: on their flat steel
doubt and suspicion are cleared away.
2.sharh: The white steel of swords, not the black ink of pages, settles every doubt. Safa'ih (blades) and saha'if (pages) have the same letters in a different order, and white is set against black.

translation: Knowledge is in the spearheads' shooting stars, flashing
between the two armies, not in the seven planets.
3.sharh: True knowledge of what will happen lies in the spearheads gleaming between two armies, not in the planets the astrologers read. He calls the spearheads shooting stars to set them against the stars of the sky.

translation: Where is the lore now, where are the stars,
and the gilding and the lies they wrought about them?
4.sharh: He mocks the astrologers: their lore, their stars and the lies they dressed up in fine words all came to nothing when the city fell.

translation: Guesswork, and stories patched together,
neither hard wood nor soft, when they are counted.
5.sharh: Their predictions are guesses and scraps stitched together. They are neither hard wood nor soft: they are nothing at all.

translation: Wonders: they claimed the days would hurry to lay them bare
in the Safar of Safars, or in Rajab.
6.sharh: They foretold wonders that the coming days would rush to reveal in Safar or in Rajab. “The Safar of Safars” magnifies the month in which they expected disaster, as one says “king of kings”.

translation: They frightened people with a dark calamity
when the western star with the tail appeared.
7.sharh: They warned that a black disaster, upheaval and the fall of rulers, would follow the rising of a comet in the west. The poet counts it among their empty predictions.

translation: They made the lofty signs of the zodiac arrange
all things, whether movable or fixed.
8.sharh: They made the signs of the zodiac the masters of events. Astrologers divided the signs into movable and fixed ones, and believed news that came under a fixed sign but doubted news under a movable one.

translation: They pass judgement in the stars' name while the stars know nothing:
none of it ever turned in a sphere or about a pole.
9.sharh: The astrologers issue verdicts in the stars' name, and the stars know nothing of them: nothing they claim was ever written in the turning of the heavens.

translation: Had the stars ever shown a thing before it came,
they would not have hidden what befell the idols and the crosses.
10.sharh: If the stars foretold anything, they would have foretold this, the greatest of conquests, which brought down the Byzantines' images and crosses. Their silence proves they foretell nothing.

translation: The conquest of conquests, too high to be encompassed
by verse strung in measure or prose from the pulpit.
11.sharh: This is the greatest of all conquests, beyond what any poem or oration can contain. Al-Suli's text has “the exalted” in place of “too high”, a verb some found too close to what is said of God.

translation: A conquest for which the gates of heaven open,
and the earth comes out in her new clothes.
12.sharh: Heaven opens its gates to it with mercy and rain, and the earth puts on new clothes, an image of the Muslims' joy. Fath (conquest) and tafattahu (open) share a root.

translation: Day of the battle of Amorium, our hopes came away
from you full-uddered, their milk sweet as honey.
13.sharh: He addresses the day itself, for its greatness. Hopes left it like camels with full udders, giving milk as sweet as honey: every wish the Muslims had was fulfilled.

translation: You left the fortune of the sons of Islam climbing
and the idolaters and their land on the way down.
14.sharh: The day left the Muslims' fortune on the rise and the unbelievers and their land sliding downhill. Sa'ad, rising ground, is set against sabab, a downward slope.

translation: A mother to them: had they hoped to ransom her,
they would have given every mother and father they had.
15.sharh: Amorium was a mother to the Byzantines, holding them as a mother holds her children. Had a ransom been possible, they would have paid it with every mother and father among them.

translation: Bare-faced, yet her taming had worn out
Khosrow, and she turned firmly away from Abu Karib.
16.sharh: Like a woman who shows her face and talks with men, yet whom no one can win, the city lay in plain view and still defeated Khosrow and spurned Abu Karib. Some take barza to mean modest.

translation: A virgin: no hand of misfortune had ever taken her,
no disaster's ambition had climbed up to her.
17.sharh: The city was a virgin, never taken: no blow of fate had touched her, and no calamity had even aspired to reach her.

translation: Since Alexander's day, or before it,
the forelocks of the nights had greyed, and hers had not.
18.sharh: Since the time of Alexander or earlier, the nights themselves had grown old and grey, while she stayed young and untouched.

translation: Until, when God had churned the years for her
as a miser churns, she was the butter of the ages.
19.sharh: God churned the years for her as a stingy woman churns milk, long and hard to get out every bit of butter, and the city was the cream of the ages. Al-Tibrizi's commentary calls it a metaphor no poet had used before.

translation: The black calamity came on them from her, heedless,
and its name was Reliever of Calamities.
20.sharh: From Amorium a black calamity fell on the Byzantines, and that same event relieved the Muslims of their troubles. Al-Suli reads it so: their disaster was the Muslims' deliverance.

translation: The omen flew against her on the day of Ankara,
when it was left with desolate squares and courtyards.
21.sharh: The omen turned against Amorium on the day Ankara fell and was left empty and desolate: her sister's ruin foretold her own.

translation: When she saw her sister ruined only yesterday,
ruin proved more catching for her than mange.
22.sharh: Amorium watched her sister city Ankara laid waste the day before, and the ruin spread to her like mange, the proverbial contagion.

translation: How many a brave horseman within her walls,
his locks dyed deep red with hot, running blood.
23.sharh: Inside her walls lay many a brave knight whose hair was dyed red by his own hot, flowing blood. Qani (deep red) and ani (boiling) chime.

translation: Dyed by the custom of the sword, his henna his own blood,
not by the custom of the faith and of Islam.
24.sharh: The fallen knight is dyed like a Muslim who reddens his grey hair with henna, but his henna is his blood, and the custom he follows is the sword's. Al-Suli's text has “the spear” for “henna”, which Abu al-Ala' thought the better match for “the sword”.

translation: Commander of the Faithful, you left in her for the fire
a day when stone and timber were laid low.
25.sharh: Turning to the caliph, he says that al-Mu'tasim gave the city to the fire, a day on which even her stone and timber submitted to the flames.

translation: You left the pitch-dark night in her as bright as forenoon,
a dawn of flame driving it from her midst.
26.sharh: The burning city turned the darkest night into broad day: a dawn made of flame drove the night out of her heart. Night is set against dawn.

translation: Until it seemed the gowns of darkness had turned
from their own colour, and the sun had never set.
27.sharh: It was as though the night's dark robes had tired of their colour and given it up, and as though the sun had not set at all.

translation: Light from the fire while the darkness stayed,
and a darkness of smoke in a wan forenoon.
28.sharh: By night the fire made light while darkness still lay all around; by day the smoke made a sickly, darkened forenoon. Night and day trade places.

translation: The sun is rising from this, though it has set,
and the sun is setting from that, though it has not.
29.sharh: From the flames the sun seems to rise after it has set; in the smoke it seems to set before it has. The first “this” is the fire, the second the smoke.

translation: Time cleared for her, as clouds clear,
to show a day of battle, pure and unclean.
30.sharh: Time parted like clouds to reveal a day at once pure and impure: pure because holy war is lawful, impure because the victors lay with the captive women that day.

translation: That day the sun rose on no man wed to a bride,
and set on no man without one.
31.sharh: By sunrise no Byzantine husband was left alive, and by sunset no Muslim soldier was without a woman, since the captives had been shared out. So al-Suli reads it.

translation: Mayya's camp, full of life, with Ghaylan walking round it,
had no fairer hills than her ruined camp.
32.sharh: Not even the beloved's encampment, full of life, as her poet-lover saw it, looked lovelier than the ruins of Amorium look to the Muslims who took it.

translation: Nor are cheeks, flushed red with shame,
more lovely to my eyes than her cheek in the dust.
33.sharh: No cheek flushed crimson with modesty pleases the poet's eye more than the city's cheek pressed into the dust. Having made Amorium a virgin bride, he gives her a cheek.

translation: An ugliness that has left our eyes no need
of any beauty to be seen, or wondrous sight.
34.sharh: The ruin is ugly to the Byzantines, yet to Muslim eyes it is enough to make every other beauty and marvel unnecessary.

translation: A happy outcome, whose fruits endure,
drew its gladness from an evil outcome.
35.sharh: The Muslims' happy end, whose fruits will last, owes its joy to the Byzantines' disastrous one. Munqalab, an outcome, closes both halves, one good and one bad.

translation: If unbelief only knew for how many ages
its fate lay in wait for it among spears and swords.
36.sharh: Unbelief had no idea how long its doom had been lying in ambush for it among spears and swords. The Byzantines were blind to what had been waiting for them.

translation: The plan of one who holds fast to God, who avenges
for God, keeps watch for God, longs for what is God's.
37.sharh: This was the work of a caliph who clings to God, takes vengeance for God, keeps God before his eyes and seeks what brings him near. His regnal title becomes a description of what he does, and God is named three times in the line.

translation: Fed on victory, his spearheads have never
grown blunt, nor been kept from the soul of one who hides.
38.sharh: Victory is his daily food, as game is a lucky hunter's. His spearheads have never grown blunt, and no fortress or armour has kept them from an enemy's life.

translation: He has raided no people and marched on no land
without an army of terror going on ahead.
39.sharh: Wherever he marched, an army of fear went before him and beat his enemies before his soldiers reached them.

translation: Had he led no host on the day of battle,
he would have gone out, himself alone, in a roaring host.
40.sharh: Even without an army he would be one: his own person is a great, clamorous host.

translation: God hurled you at her two towers and brought them down;
had any but God hurled you, you would have missed.
41.sharh: God used the caliph as His missile against the city's towers; thrown by anyone else he would have missed. His war was fought for God, and so it succeeded.

translation: After they had made her a thicket of defenders, trusting in her;
but God is the key to the gate of the tangled stronghold.
42.sharh: The Byzantines packed the city with troops until it bristled like a thicket, and trusted in it; but God opens the gate of any fortress, however dense its defenders.

translation: Their commander said, “There is no pasture near
for the grazing herds, and water is not close at hand.”
43.sharh: The Byzantine commander assured his men that the Muslims would find no grazing for their animals and no water nearby, and would soon have to leave.

translation: Wishful thinking: sword edges and the points
of the long lances robbed them of its coming true.
44.sharh: It was all wishful thinking. Sword edges and the points of long lances stripped them of what they had pictured. Salabat (robbed) and sulub (long lances) share a root.

translation: The two deaths, of white blades and of brown spears,
are the buckets that draw two lives, water and grass.
45.sharh: This answers the commander: the twin deaths dealt by sword and spear are the buckets with which the Muslims draw their two kinds of life, water and pasture. What an army needs, it wins by fighting.

translation: You answered a cry from Zibatra, and for it you spilled
the cup of sleep and the kisses of shy, loving girls.
46.sharh: When the Byzantines raided Zibatra, a captive woman cried out for al-Mu'tasim; al-Suli says the caliph answered “Here I am” and set out at once. For her he poured away sleep and the pleasures of his women.

translation: The heat of the wronged frontier posts kept you from
the coolness of mouths and their sweet water over pebbles.
47.sharh: His burning care for the violated frontier posts (thughur) kept him from the cool mouths (thughur) of his women and their sweet saliva, likened to clear water over pebbles, which are the teeth. Heat is set against cold.

translation: You answered it openly with the sword, blade drawn;
had you answered without the sword, you would not have answered.
48.sharh: He answered the cry publicly, sword drawn, and only the sword was a real answer: any other reply would have been no reply at all.

translation: Until you left the tent-pole of idolatry in the dust,
and did not stop for the pegs and ropes.
49.sharh: Idolatry is a tent: he struck at its central pole, Amorium, and laid it in the dust, without wasting time on the pegs and ropes, the villages around it. So al-Marzuqi reads it, against al-Suli.

translation: When Theophilos saw war with his own eyes,
and war, harb, takes its meaning from harab, being robbed,
50.sharh: The Byzantine emperor saw the war for himself, and knew that harb, war, is rightly named after harab, the loss of all one owns. The sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: he set out to turn its current aside with money,
but the sea, with its surging, heaving waves, overpowered him.
51.sharh: Theophilos tried to divert the flood of war by offering the caliph money to turn back, but the sea of al-Mu'tasim and his army, with its currents and rolling waves, overwhelmed him.

translation: Far from it: the steady earth was shaken under him
by a raid for God's reward, not a raid for gain.
52.sharh: No bribe could work. The solid earth shook under the emperor because of a campaign fought for God's reward, not for profit. Muhtasib (seeking God's reward) and muktasib (seeking gain) differ by one letter.

translation: He did not spend gold that outnumbers the pebbles
because he himself had need of gold.
53.sharh: The caliph had spent gold more plentiful than pebbles on the campaign; he did not do it to win the emperor's gold, and could not be bought off.

translation: Lions, the lions of the thicket, care on the day of battle
for the one they strip, not for the spoils.
54.sharh: Like a lion of the thicket, whose mind is on its prey and not on what the prey carries, the caliph wanted the enemy himself, not his money.

translation: He turned and fled, the spear having bridled his tongue
with a silence under which his insides were in uproar.
55.sharh: Theophilos fled speechless, the spear clamped on his mouth like a bit, while under that silence his heart pounded so hard it was almost audible. Silence is set against uproar.

translation: He handed his intimates death undiluted, and went off
spurring the mount most likely to save him: flight.
56.sharh: He left his closest men to be killed, handing them death neat, and rode off urging on the mount most likely to save him, which was flight itself.

translation: Bound to every hilltop, climbing it,
light with fear, not light with joy.
57.sharh: In his flight he kept climbing every rise to look back for pursuers, moving lightly, but from fear, not from the lightness of joy.

translation: If he runs from her heat as the ostrich runs,
you have filled her blaze with plenty of firewood.
58.sharh: The emperor may have escaped the heat of battle running like a male ostrich, but the caliph fed the fire with plenty of fuel: the men he left behind.

translation: Ninety thousand, like the lions of al-Shara: their skins
ripened before the figs and the grapes had ripened.
59.sharh: Ninety thousand Byzantine fighters, fierce as lions, were roasted in the fire before the figs and grapes were ripe. The Byzantines had boasted that if the Muslims stayed until then, none would get away; al-Mu'tasim answered that he hoped God would spare him the wait. Ibn al-Mu'tazz called the line base, and al-Suli defended it with this story.

translation: Many a soul, when their last root was torn out,
grew glad that, steeped in musk, would not have been glad.
60.sharh: Many a Muslim heart found its peace when the Byzantines were wiped out, a heart that no perfume, not even musk, could have sweetened before. Taba means both to be glad and to smell sweet.

translation: And many an angry man the white swords brought back,
his contentment alive from their death, his anger dead.
61.sharh: Many an angry Muslim came home from the slaughter with his anger dead and his contentment alive. Al-Suli points out the two contrasts: alive and dead, contentment and anger.

translation: While war stood up in a narrow, inescapable press
where those standing sank to their knees, abased.
62.sharh: The battle raged in a narrow press where men who had been standing fell to their knees, humbled by its weight. War stands while the standing men kneel.

translation: How much moonlike radiance was won beneath her radiance,
and under her storm cloud, how many a cool, bright smile.
63.sharh: Under the glare of battle the victors won captive women as radiant as the moon, and under its rain of death, mouths with cool, gleaming teeth. Sana is both glare and radiance, arid both a rain cloud and the side teeth.

translation: How often, in cutting the cords of necks there,
lay a cord that led to the secluded virgin.
64.sharh: Cutting through the cords of men's necks was again and again the cord that led the victors to a secluded maiden. Sabab is both a cord and a means.

translation: How many, drawn and quivering, the Indian blades won
of quivering boughs that quiver above dunes.
65.sharh: Drawn Indian swords, quivering in the hand, captured women whose figures sway like branches above hips like sand dunes. Qudub means both slender swords and slender boughs.

translation: White blades: drawn from their screens, they come back
with a better right to the fair young women than their screens.
66.sharh: When the white swords leave their sheaths, they come back with a better claim to the fair young women than the curtains that hid them. Bid means both white swords and fair women, and the word for sheaths returns at the end as the women's curtains.

translation: Caliph of God, may God reward your striving
for the root of the faith, of Islam and of honour.
67.sharh: He turns to the caliph with a prayer: may God reward him for all he has done for the faith, for Islam and for the honour of his people.

translation: You saw the great rest clearly, and saw it could not
be reached except across a bridge of toil.
68.sharh: The caliph understood that the greatest rest is reached only by crossing a bridge of hardship. Al-Suli cites an older rajaz line with the same thought: “I wore myself out on the road so as to rest”.

translation: If among the turns of fortune there is a bond of kinship
that holds, or a pledge that has not been cut,
69.sharh: If the events of time are related to one another by any lasting bond, then, as the next line says, the firmest kinship links the caliph's victories to Badr.

translation: then between your days on which you were given victory
and the days of Badr is the firmest kinship.
70.sharh: The caliph's days of victory are bound by the firmest kinship to the days of Badr, as if the conquest of Amorium were born of that first victory of Islam.

translation: They left the Sons of the Yellow One, sickly, like their name,
yellow in the face, and made the Arabs' faces shine.
71.sharh: The victories left the Byzantines, whom the Arabs called the Sons of the Yellow One, as yellow-faced as their name, with the pallor of sickness and fear, while the Arabs' faces shone.

1.1.5.head: الكُتُب
1.1.5.meaning: The books the Byzantines and the astrologers cited to show that Amorium would not fall.

3.1.3-4.meaning: “The shooting stars of the spears”: spearheads, which flash like meteors.

3.2.2.head: الخَميس
3.2.2.meaning: Khamis: an army; here the two armies facing each other.

3.2.5-6.meaning: The seven planets of the astrologers: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the sun, Venus, Mercury and the moon.

4.2.3.head: زُخرُف
4.2.3.meaning: Zukhruf: gilding; also fine words that hide a lie.

5.2.2.head: نَبع
5.2.2.meaning: Nab': a hard mountain wood used for bows.

5.2.6.head: غَرَب
5.2.6.meaning: Gharab: a soft tree that grows by rivers.

6.2.3-4.meaning: “The Safar of Safars”: Safar, the second month of the lunar year, made grand.

6.2.6.head: رَجَب
6.2.6.meaning: Rajab: the seventh month of the lunar year.

7.2.3-6.meaning: The western star with the tail: a comet.

8.1.2.head: الأَبرُج
8.1.2.meaning: Abruj: the twelve signs of the zodiac.

8.2.3.head: مُنقَلِب
8.2.3.meaning: Movable: the astrologers' name for Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn; the other signs are fixed or double.

13.1.4.head: عَمّورِيَّة
13.1.4.meaning: Amorium: a Byzantine city in Anatolia, taken by al-Mu'tasim in 223 AH (838 CE).

13.2.3.head: حافِل
13.2.3.meaning: Huffal: she-camels with udders full of milk.

16.1.1.head: بَرزَة
16.1.1.meaning: Barza: a woman who shows her face and speaks with men.

16.2.1.meaning: Kisra: Khosrow, the title of the Persian kings.

16.2.5-6.meaning: Abu Karib: one of the Tubba', the old kings of Yemen.

21.1.4.head: بَرح
21.1.4.meaning: Barh: an ill omen, from barih, a bird or beast crossing one's path on the unlucky side.

21.1.6.head: أَنقَرَة
21.1.6.meaning: Ankara: a Byzantine city taken just before Amorium; the poet Imru' al-Qays died there.

24.1.3.head: الحِنّاء
24.1.3.meaning: Henna: the Prophet's Companions dyed their grey hair with it and held it to be his custom.

30.2.6.head: جُنُب
30.2.6.meaning: Junub: in a state of impurity after intercourse, until one washes.

31.2.1-2.meaning: “Building with his wife”: a man who has taken his bride; tents were once pitched over brides.

32.1.3.head: مَيَّة
32.1.3.meaning: Mayya: the beloved of the Umayyad poet Dhu al-Rumma, who described her camp again and again.

33.2.3.head: ناظِر
33.2.3.meaning: My eye. The commentaries have nazirin, “an eye”.

37.1.2-3.meaning: Mu'tasim bi-llah: “he who holds fast to God”, the caliph's regnal title.

38.1.1-2.meaning: “Fed on victory”: from hunting, where a lucky hunter is said to be “fed” with game.

45.1.2.head: الحِمام
45.1.2.meaning: Himam: death; the two deaths come by sword and by spear.

46.1.3.head: زِبَطرِيّ
46.1.3.meaning: Of Zibatra: a frontier town between Malatya and Sumaysat, sacked by the Byzantines before the campaign.

47.1.3.head: الثُّغور
47.1.3.meaning: Thughur: the frontier posts facing Byzantium.

50.2.5.head: الحَرَب
50.2.5.meaning: Harab: being stripped of one's wealth.

55.1.4.head: الخَطِّيّ
55.1.4.meaning: Khatti: a spear, named after al-Khatt on the coast of Bahrain, where spears were traded.

56.1.3-4.meaning: “Undiluted death”: sirf is wine drunk unmixed.

58.1.6.head: الظَّليم
58.1.6.meaning: Zalim: the male ostrich, proverbial for its speed and shyness.

59.1.3-4.meaning: Al-Shara: a place known for its lions.

59.2.1.head: جُلود
59.2.1.meaning: Their skins. The commentaries have a'maruhum, “their lives”: their lives ripened, that is, ran out.

62.2.4.head: صُغر
62.2.4.meaning: Sughr: abasement. Some copies have su'ran, “proud”, and al-Suli is reported to have called sughran a misreading.

64.2.2.head: المُخَدَّرَة
64.2.2.meaning: Mukhaddara: a girl kept behind the curtain of the women's quarters.

65.1.3-4.meaning: “Indian rods”: slender swords of Indian steel.

66.2.3.head: أَتراب
66.2.3.meaning: Atrab: girls of the same age.

70.2.3.head: بَدر
70.2.3.meaning: Badr: the first victory of the Prophet and his followers over the Meccans, in 2 AH (624 CE).

71.1.2-3.meaning: Banu al-Asfar, “the Sons of the Yellow One”: the Arabs' name for the Byzantines.
